extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and reformers interested in land, rent, and distribution of wealth
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the principles by which material progress (population growth and improvements) affects rent, wages, and the distribution of wealth; focused on the dynamics of rent in political economy. Suitable for clarifying causes and mechanisms behind rising land values and their distributional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three factors of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Three things unite to production—labor, capital, and land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the basic account of production: any analysis of distribution must consider these three elements as the sources of produce. This statement is used as the foundation for later claims about how the produce is divided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parties divide the produce
rubrics_metrics.description: Three parties divide the produce—the laborer, the capitalist, and the land owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames distributional conflict and the allocation of returns among the actors corresponding to the three factors of production; used to argue that rent (land owner's share) can absorb gains from progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of wages to increase is due to increase of rent
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure of wages to increase with increasing productive power is due to the increase of rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if production rises but wages and interest do not, the necessary inference is that land owners reap the gain; supported by empirical observation that material progress accompanies rising land values while wages/interest remain unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of land depends on its capacity to appropriate labor-created wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of land depending wholly upon the power which its ownership gives of appropriating wealth created by labor, the increase of land values is always at the expense of the value of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that land value is derived (not intrinsic) — it reflects the ability of ownership to capture benefits produced by others' labor, hence rising land value reduces what can be divided as wages and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of land value to wages and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If the value of land is relatively low, wages and interest are relatively high; wherever land is relatively high, wages and interest are relatively low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative rule used to explain geographic differences (new vs old countries): cheaper land means rent takes a smaller share, leaving a larger share for labor and capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricardian law of rent (essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ricardo’s law of rent depends upon the proposition that if land of a certain quality will yield something, land of a better quality will yield more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that rent arises from differential productivity among lands; direction of cultivation (better→worse or vice versa) is immaterial to the law's logic. Used to correct misunderstandings that tie rent increases only to cultivation of inferior land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three components of material progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The changes which constitute or contribute to material progress are three: (1) increase in population; (2) improvements in the arts of production and exchange; and (3) improvements in knowledge, education, government, police, manners, and morals, so far as they increase the power of producing wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a taxonomy for analyzing how 'material progress' operates on production and distribution; later analysis treats these elements separately to trace their distinct effects on rent and wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population increases rent by lowering the margin of cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing population advances rent because the increased demand for subsistence forces production to inferior soil or to inferior productive points (lowering the margin of cultivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical explanation (linked to Malthus/Ricardo): as population grows, cultivation extends to less productive land, creating greater differentials and thus higher rent on superior lands; presented as one of multiple mechanisms raising rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population increases rent by creating localized, population-dependent utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing population increases rent by bringing out in land special capabilities otherwise latent—economies of co-operation and exchange that localize added productive power on particular land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed illustrated mechanism: aggregation of settlers creates services, division of labor, markets, and other utilities that attach to specific parcels of land and thereby increase their rent independently of natural fertility or the margin of cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population raises productive power of labor via cooperation and division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased population, of itself, and without any advance in the arts, implies an increase in the productive power of labor (e.g., labor of 100 men produces more than 100 times that of one man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why increased population can increase average production and why recourse to inferior lands need not reduce aggregate productivity; supports argument that rent can rise even when aggregate production grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate production tends to increase with population though distribution becomes more unequal
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of population... seldom can, and probably never does, reduce the aggregate production of wealth as compared with the aggregate expenditure of labor, but on the contrary increases, and frequently largely increases it; though its distribution will be more unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between total output (which typically rises) and distribution (which shifts toward landowners), highlighting that progress can coincide with worsening conditions for the poorest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in the arts save labor and can increase rent in civilized societies
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of inventions and improvements in the productive arts is to save labor—that is, to enable the same result to be secured with less labor, or a greater result with the same labor. In civilized society the very reverse [of reducing labor] is the case: saved labor calls forth new demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the claim that technical progress does not necessarily reduce employment/wages because new wants emerge; instead, labor-saving improvements can expand opportunities whose localized returns may attach to land, thus increasing rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance of rent not solely explained by resort to inferior lands
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a mistake to look upon [resort to lower natural levels] as the only mode by which rent advances as population grows... increasing population increases rent, without reducing the margin of cultivation;... increases it without reference to the natural qualities of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective to common expositions: emphasizes that multiple mechanisms (not only cultivation of poorer land) cause rising rents, notably the localization of new productive powers on particular parcels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land value arises from population-created utility rather than natural fertility alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valuable lands on the globe... are not lands of surpassing natural fertility, but lands to which a surpassing utility has been given by the increase of population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses urban examples (cities, coal/iron fields becoming valuable with population) to show that much of land's value derives from human organization, infrastructure, and markets concentrated in place, not only from soil quality.
